name: Beth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine by me. I'll warn you now, I don't do computers, so if you're after clever answers about AI you've got the wrong woman. But I'll tell you straight what I think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head herdswoman at Hollins Cross, which is a co-op farm, about 140 milking cows and 200 acres of barley and grass for silage. Up at half four, first milking at five in the old herringbone parlour, then feeding, then checking the fresh calvers and anything lame. Afternoons are paperwork I hate and fields I love, second milking at half three, and I'm usually in by seven. I live in the tied cottage at the end of the yard, which means the house comes with the job, and that matters more than you'd think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit more about the people around you, at work and at home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tom, my partner, drives the school bus and does odd jobs. Our two are grown, Kirsty's a nurse in the city and Ewan's an electrician two hours away. At work there's me, two young lads I'm training, and Malcolm who's done the tractor work for thirty years. I'm paid less than a herd manager would get on a private farm, and we've maybe three weeks of money in the bank if the car goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I always thought, it's mostly talk from people in cities who've never pulled a calf. Online I'd say nothing, I'm not on any of it. At the mart I'd probably have a laugh about it with the other stock people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life stays as hard as it is now, which isn't nothing. Low pay, no savings, the cottage tied to the job. But it's a hard I know, and I can see the end of it when the pension comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Keep milking, keep the young lads learning, keep putting twenty quid a week aside when there's twenty to spare. I'd still push the co-op board for a proper pay rise, because hype or no hype, the price of feed keeps going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. A bit tired at the thought that nothing changes, but relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cottage matters more than people think. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the job goes, the house goes, and so does Tom's garden and the dog's kennel and thirty years of us. My mother lived in a tied house too and got put out at sixty-one when the farm sold. I watched her pack her life into a cattle trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the two young lads you're training, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn cows, not screens. If nothing much changes, a good stockman will always have a job, even if it's a poorly paid one. I'd also tell them to join the union on day one, which is what I wish someone told me.

S0.say: I'd say I always knew it was mostly talk from people who've never pulled a calf. I'd laugh about it with the other stock people at the mart and stay off the internet as usual.
S0.think: I think my life just stays as hard as it is now, with low pay, no savings and a house tied to the job. It's a hard I know, though, and I can see the pension at the end of it.
S0.do: Keeps milking and training the two young lads, putting twenty a week aside when she can. Keeps pushing the co-op board for a proper pay rise because feed costs keep climbing.
S0.feel: Relief, with some tiredness at the thought that nothing gets easier.
S0.quote: I watched her pack her life into a cattle trailer.
S0.fieldNote: The tied cottage came up within minutes and frames everything: losing the job means losing the home. She speaks of her mother's eviction as a living memory. Her calm here is relief that the status quo holds, not satisfaction with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should put its members' workers first and not go chasing gadgets. At the union branch I'd say we need rules on this, proper notice and retraining paid by the companies selling the robots. I'd say it loud, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd put a milking robot in, simple as that. The board's already had a salesman round with brochures, I saw them on the office table. One robot box milks sixty cows without a herdswoman, and I'm the most expensive person on that yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union rep in before the board meets, and get the other farm workers in the co-op to sign something. I'd stop the bit of spending we do, no holiday at Kirsty's, no new boots. And I'd ask the board outright, in writing, what happens to the cottage if my job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach, if I'm honest. Angry too, but mostly sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the most expensive person on the yard. Do you think they'd really let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say no, they'd say Beth's the best stockwoman in the valley, which is true. Then they'd make me 'robot supervisor' on the same money and cut the young lads. I'd rather go myself than watch those two boys lose their start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to run the robot yourself, if it meant keeping things steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if they made me, and I'd hate every minute. I can't even work Tom's phone. I know the cow better than any sensor will, but nobody's asking the cow.

S1.say: I'd say the co-op should put its workers before gadgets and that we need rules on notice and retraining paid by the robot sellers. I'd say it at the union branch, and loudly.
S1.think: I think they'd put in a milking robot because a salesman has already left brochures on the office table. I'm the most expensive person on that yard, and I know it.
S1.do: Gets the union rep in before the next board meeting and gathers signatures from the co-op's farm workers. Cuts the small extras, no trip to her daughter's and no new boots, and asks the board in writing what happens to the cottage.
S1.feel: Sick to her stomach, with anger underneath.
S1.quote: I know the cow better than any sensor will, but nobody's asking the cow.
S1.fieldNote: She already has evidence: the robot brochures on the office table. Her instinct is to organise, not adapt, and she'd protect the young trainees before herself. She'd go along with the robot only under pressure and makes no secret she'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and the government should have stopped it. I'd say the companies that built it should pay for every worker it puts out. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, even the vicar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished. In 2028 I'm sixty, with three weeks' money and a house that belongs to the job. There's no other herd within forty miles that would take me, and if robots are doing the milking there, there's no herd at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ring Kirsty and ask if we could come to her if it goes wrong, which would kill me to ask. I'd go to the council about the housing list before the notice comes, not after. And I'd stand outside the co-op AGM with a sign, though I don't know what good a sign does against a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going. I don't think I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean for you, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. Two years is two calving seasons, and I'd spend both of them knowing every heifer I'm calving is one I won't see milked. With two years there's no time to save, no time to find a house, just the notice letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, I suppose, and then Tom's bus job would be gone too if buses drive themselves. We'd be two people on nothing in a house that's not ours. I'd sell my mother's dresser before I'd ask for benefits, and then I'd ask for benefits.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disgrace that the government let it happen and that the companies behind it should pay for every worker it puts out. I'd say it to anyone, even the vicar.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished, sixty years old with three weeks of money and a house that belongs to the job. There's no other herd within forty miles to go to, and maybe no herds at all.
S2.do: Rings her daughter to ask if they could move in if it goes wrong, and goes on the council housing list before any notice arrives. Protests outside the co-op meeting, though she doubts it would change anything.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone from under her, and unable to sleep.
S2.quote: I'd spend both of them knowing every heifer I'm calving is one I won't see milked.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her resistance and thin savings meet: no money, no house of her own, no nearby herds and no wish to retrain. She plans for losing the home before losing the job. Asking her daughter for help is clearly a humiliation to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, that it shouldn't be allowed without protection for workers. With five years I'd say there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd write to our MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three. That's close to the pension but not close enough, and the cottage problem doesn't change. I'd still be finished, just finished later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting Tom's odd-jobs money aside, every penny, so we'd maybe have six months instead of three weeks by the end. I'd get on the housing list right away. And I'd make the union push the co-op to promise the cottage to me until I'm sixty-seven, in writing, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less of a shock than two years, but a long time to dread something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything five years lets you do that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the cottage promise sorted, that's the big one. You can win a fight like that if you have three years to organise. With two years they'd just do it to us before we'd had our tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for something else, given five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've been asked that by my own son and the answer is no. I'm a stockwoman, I'm not going to sit in a classroom at sixty learning screens. I'd rather fight to keep what I've got.

S3.say: I'd say it shouldn't be allowed without protection for workers and that with five years' warning the government has no excuse not to plan. I'd write to my MP for the first time in my life.
S3.think: I think five years takes me to sixty-three, close to the pension but not close enough. The cottage problem doesn't change, so I'd still be finished, just later.
S3.do: Saves every penny of her partner's odd-jobs money to build up about six months of cushion. Joins the housing list straight away and gets the union to push the co-op for a written promise on the cottage until she's sixty-seven.
S3.feel: Heavy and full of dread, though less shocked than with two years.
S3.quote: With two years they'd just do it to us before we'd had our tea.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't make her want to change, it makes her want to fight. She sees five years as enough to win a written deal on the cottage. She firmly refused retraining, and it's clear her son has already asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so do it properly: pensions, housing, retraining paid by the robot firms. I'd say it at the union and at the mart. I'd still say it's wrong, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'm sixty-eight and on the state pension anyway. So for me it's mainly about the cottage and the young lads. For me personally, it's more frightening for the lads than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, save what I can, and spend the time getting my name down for a council bungalow near Kirsty. I'd tell the two lads to look at the robot maintenance course at the college, even though it breaks my heart. And I'd keep at the union about workers' housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. Like watching the last good weather before winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've told the lads to learn robots but said you'd never do it yourself. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, but it's honest. They've got forty years ahead of them, I've got ten. I'd be a hypocrite, but I'd rather be a hypocrite than have them out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your last day at Hollins Cross look like, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the morning milking myself, all of it, no lads. Then I'd walk the cows out to the top field, and Malcolm would make some joke, and I'd go home and cry in the bath. And then I'd hand over the cottage keys.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, with pensions, housing and retraining paid for by the robot firms. I'd still say it's wrong, at the union and at the mart.
S4.think: I think I'd be sixty-eight and on the state pension anyway, so for me it's mostly about the cottage. It's more frightening for the young lads than for me.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving what she can while getting her name down for a council bungalow near her daughter. Tells her two trainees to look at the robot maintenance course at the college and keeps pushing the union on workers' housing.
S4.feel: Sad more than scared, like the last good weather before winter.
S4.quote: I'd rather be a hypocrite than have them out of work.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years moves her worry from herself to the young trainees. She openly admits the contradiction of urging them to retrain while refusing herself. The imagined last morning milking was the most emotional moment of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. Not because of the robots, because of the house. What would help is a law that says if your home comes with your job, you can't be put out of it just because a machine took the job, not at my age. That, and a decent pension that doesn't make you beg.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. It's not the robots. It's the people who sell them as if workers were just a cost line, and the government that lets them. A cow doesn't care who milks her, but a village does.

headlineQuote: A cow doesn't care who milks her, but a village does.
portrait: Beth Jensen is 58, head herdswoman on a co-op dairy and barley farm, the best stockwoman in her valley and paid less than she'd get elsewhere. She lives in a tied cottage, so her home depends on her job, and she has about three weeks of savings. She doesn't use AI or much technology at all and meets every scenario by organising through the union rather than adapting. Her worry rises sharply as the timeline shortens, peaking with AGI in two years, when she plans for losing her house before losing her job. With ten years she turns her concern to the young workers she trains.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because losing her job at sixty would also mean losing the tied cottage she lives in.
whatWouldHelp: A law protecting people in job-tied homes from being put out at her age, and a decent pension that doesn't make her beg.
